The appeals court said it was unconstitutional to permanently disarm Edward Williams based on a 2005 DUI conviction.
The 3rd Circuit's en banc decision in Williams v. Attorney General affirms a 2023 ruling by a federal judge who likewise concluded that disarming Williams was unconstitutional. It elaborates on the logic of Range v. Attorney General, a 2023 decision that restored the gun rights of a Pennsylvania man who had been convicted of food stamp fraud. In both cases, the 3rd Circuit held that applying Section 922(g)(1) to the plaintiffs was not "consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation"—the Second Amendment test established by the Supreme Court's 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. jina.title: The 3rd Circuit Upholds the Gun Rights of a Man Who Committed a Nonviolent Misdemeanor 2 Decades Ago
jina.snippet:
Thanks to a 2005 DUI conviction in Pennsylvania, Edward Williams permanently lost the constitutional right to keep and bear arms. But he did not realize that until a decade later, and his confusion on that point is understandable.

The federal law that stripped Williams of his Second Amendment rights is commonly described as applying to "felons," and Williams' offense was a misdemeanor. But although his sentence did not include any time behind bars, his crime theoretically _could_ have sent him to prison for up to five years. That was enough to trigger [18 USC 922(g)(1)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/922), which covers anyone convicted of "a crime punishable by imprisonment for a term exceeding one year."

When a lawyer alerted Williams to that wrinkle, which made his continued ownership of firearms a federal felony, he got rid of his guns. But he did not think that requirement was fair, reasonable, or constitutional, and this week a federal appeals court agreed. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit recognized a historical tradition of disarming "physically dangerous individuals" whose possession of firearms would pose a threat to public safety. But it said Williams plainly does not fit into that category.

"The federal government spent nearly a decade trying to permanently disarm a peaceable man over a nonviolent misdemeanor—and it lost bigly," [says](https://www.firearmspolicy.org/another-fpc-win-third-circuit-strikes-down-federal-lifetime-gun-ban-over-dui-in-fpc-backed-challenge-to-gun-control-act) Brandon Combs, president of the Firearms Policy Coalition, which [supported](https://www.firearmspolicy.org/fpc-brief-federal-lifetime-gun-ban-is-unconstitutional) Williams' lawsuit. "The government does not get to turn a nonviolent conviction into a lifetime ban on exercising a constitutionally protected right."

Before: CHAGARES, Chief Judge, HARDIMAN, SHWARTZ,
KRAUSE, RESTREPO, BIBAS, PORTER, MATEY, PHIPPS,
FREEMAN, MONTGOMERY-REEVES, CHUNG, BOVE, and
MASCOTT, Circuit Judges.
Argued Feb. 11, 2026
Decided Oct. 13, 2026

Edward Williams had two
convictions for driving under the influence of alcohol in the
early 2000s, the second of which (unbeknownst to him)
triggered 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1), which purports to make it
“unlawful” for persons convicted of “a crime punishable by
imprisonment for a term exceeding one year” to possess
firearms. Seeking to restore his rights, Williams filed for a
declaratory judgment to confirm that § 922(g)(1), as applied to
him, runs afoul of the Second Amendment. The District Court
agreed with Williams, and we will affirm that judgment.

For these reasons, I would hold that Williams is excused
from exhausting his remedy under section 925(c).

Unlike the Majority, I conclude that Williams’s request
for a declaration that he is not subject to the felon firearm
possession ban in 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) fails.  First, Williams
has a felony-equivalent DUI conviction1
that bans him from
possessing firearms.  Second, he failed to exhaust his
administrative remedy under 18 U.S.C. § 925(c) before
seeking court intervention.  As a result, I would vacate the
order granting Williams a declaratory judgment and direct the
District Court to dismiss his complaint without prejudice so
that he can pursue relief under § 925(c).

For the reasons set forth herein, and in Holloway, I
conclude that Williams’s DUI conviction disarms him
consistently with the Second Amendment.8

The federal government can disarm a man convicted of making terroristic threats but not someone who merely has a criminal history of drunk driving, the Third Circuit ruled as a whole court in separate decisions Tuesday.
The decisions clarify the appeals court’s stance on an area of gun law that’s been hotly debated in recent years: which kinds of felony convictions should disqualify someone from gun ownership under the Second Amendment.
“The right to keep and bear arms has limits, and this is one: Those who pose a risk of physical violence from misusing guns can be disarmed before that risk becomes a reality,” wrote Judge Stephanos Bibas for the majority of the en banc court in the terroristic threats case, US v. Bost .
Certain “violent” convictions are, on their face, enough to show a risk that someone will misuse guns, he wrote, and that includes the terroristic threat felony underlying defendant James Bost’s case.
But in the DUI-related matter, Williams v. Attorney General , the en banc majority sided with Edward Williams , saying that the “felony” label “captures conduct that would have commonly justified exclusion” from gun ownership but also “a host of less significant acts.”

UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE
THIRD CIRCUIT
No. 24-1091
EDWARD A. WILLIAMS
V.
ATTORNEY GENERAL UNITED STATES OF AMERICA;
DIRECTOR BUREAU OF ALCOHOL TOBACCO FIREARMS &
EXPLOSIVES; DIRECTOR FEDERAL BUREAU OF
INVESTIGATION; UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,
Appellants
_____________________________
On Appeal from U.S. District Court, E.D. Pa.
Judge John M. Younge, No. 2:17-cv-02641
Before: CHAGARES, Chief Judge, HARDIMAN, SHWARTZ,
KRAUSE, RESTREPO, BIBAS, PORTER, MATEY, PHIPPS,
FREEMAN, MONTGOMERY-REEVES, CHUNG, BOVE, and
MASCOTT, Circuit Judges.
Argued Feb. 11, 2026
Decided Oct. 13, 2026

Edward Williams had two
convictions for driving under the influence of alcohol in the
early 2000s, the second of which (unbeknownst to him)
triggered 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1), which purports to make it
“unlawful” for persons convicted of “a crime punishable by
imprisonment for a term exceeding one year” to possess
firearms. Seeking to restore his rights, Williams filed for a
declaratory judgment to confirm that § 922(g)(1), as applied to
him, runs afoul of the Second Amendment. The District Court
agreed with Williams, and we will affirm that judgment.

For these reasons, I would hold that Williams is excused
from exhausting his remedy under section 925(c).

Unlike the Majority, I conclude that Williams’s request
for a declaration that he is not subject to the felon firearm
possession ban in 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1) fails.  First, Williams
has a felony-equivalent DUI conviction1
that bans him from
possessing firearms.  Second, he failed to exhaust his
administrative remedy under 18 U.S.C. § 925(c) before
seeking court intervention.  As a result, I would vacate the
order granting Williams a declaratory judgment and direct the
District Court to dismiss his complaint without prejudice so
that he can pursue relief under § 925(c).

For the reasons set forth herein, and in Holloway, I
conclude that Williams’s DUI conviction disarms him
consistently with the Second Amendment.8
